name: Question 11
problem:
Suppose that $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$, has exponential order $a,$ and its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for $s>a.$ Then, $F(s)$ is differentiable at every point $s>a,$ and we have

$$
{F}^{′}(s)=-\,L{t\cdot f(t)}.
$$

A proof of this statement is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ $F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t$ exists for $s>a.$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${F}^{′}(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${F}^{′}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{∂}{∂s}({e}^{-st}f(t))\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $\frac{∂}{∂s}({e}^{-st}f(t))=-t{e}^{-st}f(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${F}^{′}(s)=-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }t{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${F}^{′}(s)=-L{t\cdot f(t)}$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ and
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ and {{field-3}}.

Question 11
?
Suppose that f(t) is piecewise continuous on [0,∞), has exponential order a, and its Laplace transform F(s)=L{f(t)} exists for s>a. Then, F(s) is differentiable at every point s>a, and we have F′(s)=−L{t⋅f(t)}.

A proof of this statement is given below.

L1: F(s)=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt exists for s>a.

L2: F′(s)=dds∫0∞e−stf(t)dt

L3: F′(s)=∫0∞∂∂s(e−stf(t))dt

L4: ∂∂s(e−stf(t))=−te−stf(t)

L5: F′(s)=−∫0∞te−stf(t)dt

L6: F′(s)=−L{t⋅f(t)}

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

The integral in line L1 converges since
 
t≥0
f is bounded on [0,∞)
f is of exponential order and is piecewise continuous
the Laplace transform is linear
e−st is infinitely differentiable
.

Line L2 follows from line L1 and
 
integration by parts
differentiating under the integral sign
the definition of the Laplace transform
the definition of the derivative with respect to s
.

Line L3 follows from L2 and
 
integration by parts
the continuity of partial derivatives
differentiating under the integral sign
.
